name: shrink-to-fit
intent: Return a container's over-allocated storage to the amount its current elements actually need, so the memory reserved for a past peak is released once the container has shrunk.
problem: A growable container sizes its storage for the largest element count it ever held: after a bulk load, a burst or a fan-in, removing elements lowers the size but not the allocation, so a long-lived list, buffer or map keeps holding peak-shaped memory that nothing uses. The container looks small to every reader of its size while its footprint stays at the peak, and enough such containers turn a memory budget that was sized for live data into one that dies at the peak.
context: Containers whose storage is amortized and observable - dynamic arrays, strings and builders, array-backed maps - that stay alive after their shrink phase: caches and registries after eviction, buffers after a spiky ingest, parsed documents after filtering, per-connection or per-tenant structures after churn. Most relevant when memory is the binding resource (long-running services, embedded budgets, many containers per process) and when the container has a visible size/capacity split; least relevant when a pool, arena or garbage collector owns the storage instead.
benefits: Releases storage that was sized for a peak that no longer exists: steady-state memory follows live data instead of high-water marks.
Restores the invariant capacity ~ size, which makes per-container memory accounting and sizing estimates meaningful again.
Stops one oversized buffer from pinning a whole allocation class, page or arena segment in the allocators and collectors that reclaim at block granularity.
Cheap and local: one call, one swap or one realloc in the container's own module - no interface, protocol or ownership change.
Fits an explicit lifecycle boundary (after load, filter, eviction or publish), where the cost is paid once and can be measured, instead of being paid implicitly at an unpredictable peak.
tradeoffs: The guarantee is usually non-binding or implementation-defined - C++: 'It depends on the implementation whether the request is fulfilled'; C# does nothing once the list is above ~90% of capacity; Rust: 'the resulting vector might still have some excess capacity' - so a hard memory budget cannot be built on it.

Reallocation invalidates iterators, pointers, references and views into the container, so a local-looking call is an API-visible event: concurrent readers, cached pointers and stored slices must be quiesced or re-derived.

Copy-based realizations (swap with a temporary, rebuild, realloc that cannot contract in place) need a second allocation the size of the live range at exactly the moment memory is tightest, and in C the realloc can fail there.

It destroys the growth slack that made appends amortized O(1): trimming inside a mutation loop turns appends into repeated O(n) copies, so the pattern is a pessimization wherever the container is about to grow again.

Reclamation is not release: the allocator, the garbage collector, or a surviving subslice, view or buffer export decides whether bytes actually return, so RSS may not move even when the capacity number does.
Rebuild-based realizations replace the object rather than shrinking it: every other holder keeps the peak allocation alive, and writers on the two references diverge silently.
In runtimes where capacity is invisible or ignored (plain JavaScript arrays, Kotlin/JS) the operation is unobservable, so defensive trims accumulate as cargo cult with nothing to measure.

participants.responsibility: Owns the element sequence and the allocated storage; its size is data while its capacity is slack, and it is the only thing that can turn unused capacity into free storage.

Knows that the growth phase has ended, chooses the quiescent point for the trim, and is responsible for dropping or re-acquiring every iterator, pointer, view and live copy of the container before and after it.
Carries out the reallocation or declines to: realloc, the container's trim call, the garbage collector that collects a rebuilt array. The actual guarantee lives here, not in the pattern.

use_cases: A per-connection or per-session receive/send buffer that absorbed one large burst and then must sit idle for hours; the idle footprint should not be the burst size.
A cache or registry that evicted most of its entries after a churn phase but keeps its array-backed storage at the peak entry count.
A batch import: build a large collection from an input file, filter it down to the survivors, and keep the result for the process lifetime.
Serialization: build a response payload in memory, then hold it while a slow consumer drains it - trimming to size lowers steady-state memory across thousands of in-flight responses.
Multi-tenant services where each tenant's peak must not become its permanent footprint, and per-tenant accounting would otherwise show phantom usage.
Embedded, edge or console targets with a fixed memory budget where a peak-phase container must hand its storage back before the next phase starts.

Rust std makes the pattern an explicit API: std::vec::Vec never auto-shrinks (to avoid unnecessary allocations/deallocations), so long-lived buffers call Vec::shrink_to_fit once a load or drain phase ends, and owners that want storage exactly the size of the data convert with into_boxed_slice - its documented property is that len == capacity makes the Vec <-> Box<[T]> round trip reallocation-free.

The JDK ships the canonical form as java.util.ArrayList.trimToSize(): the javadoc's stated purpose is to minimize memory usage by trimming the internal array to the list's current size once the ArrayList is known not to grow - the standard closing move for startup-built lookup lists, static tables and caches.

.NET collections expose the operation as TrimExcess (List<T>, Queue<T>, SortedList<TKey,TValue>): Microsoft's documented guidance is to call it when no more elements will be added, with a built-in cost guard - the trim is skipped entirely once the collection is more than 90% full.
avoid_when: The container will grow again immediately (next batch, next request, next level): the slack is the optimization - reserve up front or reuse the container instead of trimming between phases.

You need a guaranteed bound: the operation is usually a request the runtime may decline, so size the storage up front (reserve/with_capacity/ensureCapacity) or use an allocator or pool with explicit accounting.
The storage is not the container's: arena, pool or slab-allocated buffers return to their owner, and trimming inside a pooled object either does nothing or fights the pool's own lifecycle.

The runtime already manages the storage and capacity is not observable or not honored (plain JavaScript arrays, Kotlin/JS, garbage-collected runtimes that reclaim whole segments): a copy to shrink is just a copy.
The trim would run on a hot path or under memory pressure: the copy-based forms cost a second allocation of the same magnitude exactly when that is most dangerous.
anti_patterns: Shrinking after every removal or append: the container reallocates on each mutation, so a benign O(n) fill becomes quadratic and latency spikes at the worst moment.

Deciding a memory budget on the assumption that the trim worked: most realizations are non-binding requests or heuristics (C# skips the reallocation above 90% of capacity), and the capacity may stay at the peak.

Holding raw pointers, iterators, String views or memoryviews across the trim and dereferencing them afterwards - the classic use-after-free/undefined-behaviour form of 'we only wanted to save memory'.
Copying to shrink while another reference still points at the old container or its buffer: nothing is released, and the two now-divergent views are the next bug.
Shrinking the view instead of the owner (Go subslice cap, JS subarray, ArraySlice-style views): the small handle keeps the whole peak allocation alive, which is the opposite of the intent.
Trimming on a request path where the copy is paid by the user (p99 latency) rather than once at a lifecycle boundary.
design_principles: Separate what a container can hold from how much it actually holds: size and capacity are different facts, and only one of them is the live data.
Release resources at the end of the phase that needed them - tie storage to the lifecycle of the peak, not to the identity of the object.
Make the cost explicit and local: convert an invisible slow leak into a measured, deliberate one-off operation at a quiescent point.
Single responsibility: the container owns storage, the owner decides when growth has ended, and the allocator decides what reclamation means - do not blur these roles.
best_practices: Trim at quiescent boundaries - after a load, filter, eviction or publish phase, or immediately before handing the structure to a long-lived owner - never inside a mutation loop.
Quiesce first: no iterator, pointer, view, span or buffer export into the container may survive the call; re-acquire after it and document the invalidation for callers.

Verify the effect where the language exposes it (capacity(), Count/Capacity, len/cap, sys.getsizeof) and know where it cannot be verified (JS, Kotlin/JS, non-binding requests) so the intent is not mistaken for a guarantee.

Reclaim for real: drop subslices, views and second references to the old storage, and clear the old object - a trimmed header, a linked buffer or another holder keeps the peak alive and makes the trim cosmetic.
Prefer right-sizing up front for repeated phases (reserve/with_capacity/ensureCapacity, sized constructors) and pooling of containers over repeated shrink-then-grow cycles.

Do not schedule the trim when memory is tightest: the copy-based forms hold both buffers at once, so run them while there is headroom or use a variant that keeps a floor instead of trimming to the bone.
Trim is not erase: freed storage may still contain the old values, so overwrite or zero sensitive buffers before letting them go.
sources: More C++ Idioms (Wikibooks), chapter 'Shrink-to-fit' - intent 'Minimize the capacity of a container just enough to hold existing range'; also known as 'Swap-To-Fit', introduced by Scott Meyers in Effective STL; motivation: containers allocate more memory than the elements they hold, and the leftover capacity after a container shrinks 'can be unnecessary wastage of memory resources'; the pre-C++11 sample std::vector<int>(v).swap(v) with the more reliable range-constructor form, and the C++11 note that vector, deque and basic_string declare shrink_to_fit() as a non-binding request: https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/More_C%2B%2B_Idioms/Shrink-to-fit

cppreference, std::vector<T,Allocator>::shrink_to_fit - 'Requests the removal of unused capacity. It is a non-binding request to reduce capacity() to size(). It depends on the implementation whether the request is fulfilled'; if reallocation occurs all iterators and references (including end()) are invalidated; complexity at most linear; also documents that shrink_to_fit() is not available in libstdc++ C++98 mode: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector/shrink_to_fit

Scott Meyers, Effective STL (2001) - source of the 'swap-to-fit' alias per the Wikibooks chapter above (the chapter's footnote links the book's errata page, which discusses the string(s.begin(), s.end()).swap(s) form: http://www.aristeia.com/BookErrata/estl1e-errata.html)

std::vec::Vec - Rust standard library documentation - Vec does not auto-shrink 'to avoid unnecessary allocations/deallocations'; shrink_to_fit may shrink in place or reallocate and 'the resulting vector might still have some excess capacity' depending on the allocator; when len == capacity the Vec <-> Box<[T]> conversion does not reallocate, which into_boxed_slice leverages: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/vec/struct.Vec.html

java.util.ArrayList - Oracle Java SE 24 API documentation - trimToSize(): 'Trims the capacity of this ArrayList instance to be the list's current size'; the documented way for an application to minimize storage once the list is known not to grow: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/24/docs/api/java.base/java/util/ArrayList.html

Microsoft Learn, Queue<T>.TrimExcess Method - reduces capacity to the element count only if Count is less than 90% of Capacity, otherwise the call does nothing; O(n); documented to be called when no more elements will be added - the same TrimExcess/90%-threshold design applies across the collection family (List<T>, SortedList<TKey,TValue>): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.queue-1.trimexcess?view=net-10.0

The Go Blog, 'Go Slices: usage and internals' - a slice is a pointer/length/capacity descriptor; reslicing without copying may leave the whole (larger) backing array in memory holding more data than the active portion, and copying the subset to a new slice is the documented way to release the unused capacity: https://go.dev/blog/slices-intro

Go Wiki, SliceTricks - the canonical catalog of copy-based slice operations (extend, copy, filter), including the append(make([]T, 0, n), a...) form used to move elements onto right-sized storage: https://go.dev/wiki/SliceTricks

WG21 LWG Issue 755, 'std::vector and std::string lack explicit shrink-to-fit operations' - the standardization origin of shrink_to_fit: before it, shrink-to-fit existed only as idioms (swap with a copy; string::reserve(0)), and the adopted member was deliberately specified as a non-binding request: https://wg21.cmeerw.net/lwg/issue755

P0966R0, 'basic_string::reserve Should Not Shrink' - WG21 paper behind the C++17 change that made reserve(0) no longer shrink-to-fit, an explicit rejection of reserve-as-trim: https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2018/p0966r0.html

B. Vorbrodt, 'shrink_to_fit that doesn't suck' (2019) - misuse analysis: naive or aggressive shrinking can worsen performance and memory (allocator granularity floors, page faults, repeated copies for sub-granularity savings); the non-binding wording exists so the allocator can decline, and shrinking inside repeated-resize code is the classic anti-pattern: https://vorbrodt.blog/2019/01/27/shrink_to_fit-that-doesnt-suck/
